Edge cases to test:

  • Prices only fall → 0.
  • A single day → 0.
  • The minimum comes after the maximum, e.g. [3, 5, 1] → 2 (not 4).

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Easy 219. Contains Duplicate II Google ArrayHash Set

Problem: Return True if there are two indices i ≠ j with nums[i] == nums[j] and |i − j| ≤ k.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,3,1], k = 3
Output: true
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,0,1,1], k = 1
Output: true

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · -10⁹ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹ · 0 ≤ k ≤ 10⁵

Hint 1

"Within distance k" means inside a window of the last k positions.

Hint 2

Keep those values in a set; when the window grows past k, remove the one that fell out.

From brute force to the pattern: Comparing every pair within distance k is O(n · k). A set holding just the current window answers "seen recently?" in O(1): O(n).

Spot it: "Within distance k" = within a window of the last k elements. Keep those values in a set: a value already in the set is a close duplicate.

Approach:

  1. Walk the array. The set window holds the values of the previous k positions.
  2. If nums[i] is already in window, a duplicate within distance k exists: return True.
  3. Add nums[i]. If the window now holds more than k values, remove the one that just fell out, nums[i − k].
  4. If the loop ends, no close duplicate exists.
class Solution:
    def containsNearbyDuplicate(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> bool:
        # the values of the last k positions
        window = set()
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            if nums[i] in window:
                # the same value appeared at most k positions ago
                return True
            window.add(nums[i])
            if len(window) > k:
                # nums[i - k] is now too far away to pair with anything ahead
                window.remove(nums[i - k])
        return False

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. window = set(): at most k values, the ones close enough to pair with the current position.
  2. if nums[i] in window: return True: an O(1) set lookup finds a duplicate within distance k.
  3. window.add(nums[i]): the current value joins the window for the positions that follow.
  4. if len(window) > k: window.remove(nums[i - k]): keep the window at k values. The window never holds a duplicate (we would have returned), so its size equals the number of positions it covers.
  5. return False: no pair was close enough.

Dry run on the example:

nums = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3], k = 2 (LeetCode Example 3). Returns False: equal values are always 3 apart.

inums[i]in window?window after (size ≤ k)
01no{1}
12no{1, 2}
23noadd 3, too big → remove nums[0] = 1 → {2, 3}
31noadd 1 → remove nums[1] = 2 → {3, 1}
42noadd 2 → remove nums[2] = 3 → {1, 2}
53noadd 3 → remove nums[3] = 1 → {2, 3}

The loop ends without a hit, so the answer is False. With nums = [1, 2, 3, 1], k = 3 the second 1 would find the first one still in the window.

Edge cases to test:

  • k = 0 → always False.
  • The duplicate exactly k apart → True.
  • Duplicates only further apart than k → False.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(k) space.

Hard 30. Substring with Concatenation of All Words Google StringHash Map

Problem: words are all the same length. Return every starting index in s of a substring that is some concatenation of all the words, each used exactly as many times as it appears in words (any order).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "barfoothefoobarman", words = ["foo","bar"]
Output: [0,9]
Explanation: The substring starting at 0 is "barfoo". It is the concatenation of ["bar","foo"] which is a permutation of words. The substring starting at 9 is "foobar". It is the concatenation of ["foo","bar"] which is a permutation of words.
Example 2
Input: s = "wordgoodgoodgoodbestword", words = ["word","good","best","word"]
Output: []
Explanation: There is no concatenated substring.

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁴ · 1 ≤ words.length ≤ 5000 · 1 ≤ words[i].length ≤ 30 · s and words[i] consist of lowercase English letters.

Hint 1

All words have the same length L. Read s in chunks of L characters.

Hint 2

Run a sliding window whose unit is one word, once for each starting offset 0..L − 1, with a count map of the words inside.

From brute force to the pattern: Checking every start index by slicing len(words) words and comparing counts is O(n · m · L). A word-sized sliding window per offset reuses the counts as it moves, so each word slice is handled a constant number of times: O(n · L).

Spot it: "Contiguous substring" + "contains exactly these counts" → a variable sliding window with a count map, like Minimum Window Substring. The twist: the window's unit is a whole word of length L, so it moves in jumps of L.

Key insight: A match can start at any index, but jumping by L only visits indices with the same remainder mod L. So run the word-sized window L times, once for each offset 0 .. L − 1. Each run is linear.

Approach:

  1. Count how many times each word is needed (need).
  2. For each offset 0 .. L − 1: start an empty window at left = offset and read words at right = offset, offset + L, ….
  3. If the word is not in need, no answer can include it. Clear the window and restart just after it.
  4. Otherwise add it to seen. If that word now appears too often, drop words from the left until it doesn't.
  5. If the window holds exactly len(words) words, record left, then drop one word from the left to keep searching.
class Solution:
    def findSubstring(self, s: str, words: List[str]) -> List[int]:
        word_len = len(words[0])
        total_words = len(words)
        # how many copies of each word a valid window must contain
        need = {}
        for w in words:
            need[w] = need.get(w, 0) + 1
        result = []
        # the window jumps a whole word at a time, so try every starting offset
        for offset in range(word_len):
            left = offset
            seen = {}    # word counts inside the current window
            count = 0    # number of words in the current window
            for right in range(offset, len(s) - word_len + 1, word_len):
                word = s[right:right + word_len]
                if word not in need:
                    # this word can never be part of an answer: restart after it
                    seen = {}
                    count = 0
                    left = right + word_len
                    continue
                seen[word] = seen.get(word, 0) + 1
                count = count + 1
                # too many copies of this word: shrink from the left until it fits again
                while seen[word] > need[word]:
                    left_word = s[left:left + word_len]
                    seen[left_word] = seen[left_word] - 1
                    count = count - 1
                    left = left + word_len
                if count == total_words:
                    # every word is present the right number of times
                    result.append(left)
                    # drop the leftmost word and keep sliding
                    left_word = s[left:left + word_len]
                    seen[left_word] = seen[left_word] - 1
                    count = count - 1
                    left = left + word_len
        return result

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. need: a count map of the words, e.g. {"foo": 1, "bar": 1}. Words can repeat, so this must be a count, not a set.
  2. for offset in range(word_len): answers can start at any index, but one pass of jumps only reaches indices with the same remainder. word_len passes cover them all.
  3. for right in range(offset, len(s) - word_len + 1, word_len): right is the start of the next word to bring into the window.
  4. if word not in need: a foreign word poisons every window containing it, so reset and start the window after it.
  5. seen[word] = seen.get(word, 0) + 1, count = count + 1: grow the window by one word.
  6. while seen[word] > need[word]: the new word appears too often; remove words from the left (updating seen and count) until it fits.
  7. if count == total_words: the window is a full concatenation: record its start, then drop its first word so the search continues.

Dry run on the example:

s = "barfoothefoobarman", words = ["foo", "bar"] (LeetCode Example 1). word_len = 3. Returns [0, 9]. Offset 0 finds both answers; offsets 1 and 2 find nothing.

rightwordwhat happenswindow afterresult
0"bar"addbar (left = 0)[]
3"foo"add → 2 words = all words → record 0, drop barfoo (left = 3)[0]
6"the"not a needed word → resetempty (left = 9)[0]
9"foo"addfoo (left = 9)[0]
12"bar"add → 2 words → record 9, drop foobar (left = 12)[0, 9]
15"man"not a needed word → resetempty (left = 18)[0, 9]

Edge cases to test:

  • Repeated words in words, e.g. ["foo", "foo"].
  • A foreign word in the middle resets the window.
  • s shorter than all the words together → [].

Complexity: O(n · L) time: L offsets, each scanning about n / L words, and slicing a word costs O(L). O(m) space for the two maps, where m is the number of words.

Medium 395. Longest Substring with At Least K Repeating Characters Google StringHash Map

Problem: Return the length of the longest substring in which every character appears at least k times.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "aaabb", k = 3
Output: 3
Explanation: The longest substring is "aaa", as 'a' is repeated 3 times.
Example 2
Input: s = "ababbc", k = 2
Output: 5
Explanation: The longest substring is "ababb", as 'a' is repeated 2 times and 'b' is repeated 3 times.

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁴ · s consists of only lowercase English letters. · 1 ≤ k ≤ 10⁵

Hint 1

Why doesn't a normal sliding window work here?

Hint 2

Fix the number of distinct letters t in the window (1 to 26) and run a window for each t.

From brute force to the pattern: Checking every substring is O(n²). Fixing the number of distinct letters makes the window monotonic, giving 26 linear passes.

Spot it: A plain window fails: adding a character can make the window invalid or valid, so it's not monotonic. Fixing the number of distinct letters t restores monotonicity: for each t in 1..26, keep a window with at most t distinct letters and check whether all of them reach k.

Why not another pattern? Divide and conquer also works: any character with total count < k can't be in the answer, so split the string around it and recurse (O(26 · n) too). Checking every substring is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. For each target from 1 to 26 (number of distinct letters allowed):
  2. Slide a window: add s[right]; while the window has more than target distinct letters, shrink from the left.
  3. Track distinct and at_least_k (letters whose count reached k). If both equal target, the window is valid.
  4. Keep the longest valid window over all targets.
class Solution:
    def longestSubstring(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
        best = 0
        for target in range(1, 27):  # exactly `target` distinct letters in the window
            count = [0] * 26
            distinct = 0  # letters present in the window
            at_least_k = 0  # letters present at least k times
            left = 0
            for right in range(len(s)):
                c = ord(s[right]) - ord("a")
                if count[c] == 0:
                    distinct = distinct + 1
                count[c] = count[c] + 1
                if count[c] == k:
                    at_least_k = at_least_k + 1
                while distinct > target:  # too many letters: shrink
                    d = ord(s[left]) - ord("a")
                    if count[d] == k:
                        at_least_k = at_least_k - 1
                    count[d] = count[d] - 1
                    if count[d] == 0:
                        distinct = distinct - 1
                    left = left + 1
                if distinct == target and at_least_k == target:
                    best = max(best, right - left + 1)  # every letter appears >= k times
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The outer loop fixes how many different letters the window may contain; with that fixed, "too many letters" is a monotonic condition again.
  2. distinct and at_least_k are updated exactly when a count crosses 0 or k, so both stay O(1) per step.
  3. The inner while restores "at most target distinct letters" by shrinking from the left.
  4. A window is valid when it has exactly target letters and all of them reached k.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k = 1 → the whole string.
  • k larger than the string → 0.
  • A letter that appears fewer than k times splits the string.

Complexity: O(26 · n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 413. Arithmetic Slices Google Array

Problem: Count the contiguous subarrays of length ≥ 3 whose consecutive differences are all equal.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,3,4]
Output: 3
Explanation: We have 3 arithmetic slices in nums: [1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4] and [1,2,3,4] itself.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1]
Output: 0

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 5000 · -1000 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 1000

Hint 1

Look at runs of equal differences. How many slices does a run of length L contain?

Hint 2

Walk the array; each time the run grows, the number of slices ending at the new element goes up by one.

From brute force to the pattern: Testing every subarray is O(n²). A run of length L contains (L−1)(L−2)/2 slices, and counting them incrementally as the run grows takes one pass.

Spot it: Arithmetic slices live inside maximal runs with a constant difference. Extending a run by one element creates new slices that end at that element: a window that grows while the difference stays the same.

Why not another pattern? Checking every subarray is O(n²) (or O(n³) naively). This is also a tiny DP: dp[i] = dp[i − 1] + 1 when the difference repeats.

Approach:

  1. current = number of arithmetic slices ending at the current index.
  2. If nums[i] − nums[i−1] == nums[i−1] − nums[i−2], every slice ending at i − 1 extends, plus one new length-3 slice: current += 1.
  3. Otherwise the run breaks: current = 0. Add current to the total each step.
class Solution:
    def numberOfArithmeticSlices(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        total = 0
        current = 0  # arithmetic slices ending at index i
        for i in range(2, len(nums)):
            if nums[i] - nums[i - 1] == nums[i - 1] - nums[i - 2]:
                current = current + 1  # the run grows: one more slice ends here than before
            else:
                current = 0  # the difference changed: the run is broken
            total = total + current
        return total

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Start at index 2: a slice needs three elements.
  2. Same difference as before: all slices ending at i − 1 extend to i, and [i−2, i−1, i] is new, hence + 1.
  3. A different difference resets the run.
  4. total accumulates the slices ending at each index.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Fewer than 3 elements → 0.
  • One long run, e.g. [1, 2, 3, 4] → 3.
  • Constant arrays (difference 0) count too.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 713. Subarray Product Less Than K Google Array

Problem: Count the contiguous subarrays whose product is strictly less than k (all numbers are positive).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [10,5,2,6], k = 100
Output: 8
Explanation: The 8 subarrays that have product less than 100 are: [10], [5], [2], [6], [10, 5], [5, 2], [2, 6], [5, 2, 6] Note that [10, 5, 2] is not included as the product of 100 is not strictly less than k.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,2,3], k = 0
Output: 0

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 3 * 10⁴ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 1000 · 0 ≤ k ≤ 10⁶

Hint 1

With positive numbers, a window's product grows as it expands and shrinks as it contracts.

Hint 2

For each right edge, shrink the window until valid; then all subarrays ending there and starting inside it count.

From brute force to the pattern: Multiplying out every subarray is O(n²). The window stays valid as it slides, and counting right − left + 1 per step counts all valid subarrays in one pass.

Spot it: Positive numbers mean the product only grows when the window grows and only shrinks when it shrinks: a variable sliding window. When the window [left, right] is valid, every subarray ending at right inside it is valid too.

Why not another pattern? Checking all subarrays is O(n²). Logarithms plus prefix sums and binary search work but add floating-point risk and log n.

Approach:

  1. If k ≤ 1, no product of positive integers is below it: return 0.
  2. Extend right, multiplying product by nums[right].
  3. While product ≥ k, divide out nums[left] and move left right.
  4. Add right − left + 1: the number of valid subarrays ending at right.
class Solution:
    def numSubarrayProductLessThanK(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        if k <= 1:
            return 0  # products of positive integers are at least 1
        product = 1
        left = 0
        count = 0
        for right in range(len(nums)):
            product = product * nums[right]  # grow the window
            while product >= k:
                product = product // nums[left]  # shrink until valid again
                left = left + 1
            count = count + (right - left + 1)  # subarrays ending at right
        return count

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. k <= 1 guard: otherwise the shrinking loop could move left past right.
  2. Multiplying by nums[right] adds the new element to the window's product.
  3. The while divides out elements from the left until the product is below k again (exact integer division because nums[left] divides the product).
  4. right - left + 1: subarrays [left..right], [left+1..right], …, [right..right] all have product < k.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k = 0 or k = 1 → 0.
  • A single element ≥ k (the window becomes empty).
  • All ones with k = 2 → n(n + 1)/2.

Complexity: O(n) time (each index enters and leaves the window once), O(1) space.

Medium 718. Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray Google Array

Problem: Return the length of the longest subarray that appears in both nums1 and nums2.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums1 = [1,2,3,2,1], nums2 = [3,2,1,4,7]
Output: 3
Explanation: The repeated subarray with maximum length is [3,2,1].
Example 2
Input: nums1 = [0,0,0,0,0], nums2 = [0,0,0,0,0]
Output: 5
Explanation: The repeated subarray with maximum length is [0,0,0,0,0].

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums1.length, nums2.length ≤ 1000 · 0 ≤ nums1[i], nums2[i] ≤ 100

Hint 1

A common subarray means a run of equal elements when the arrays are aligned at the right offset.

Hint 2

Try every offset and find the longest streak of matches on it (or use the DP on (i, j)).

From brute force to the pattern: Comparing every pair of start positions and extending is O(m · n · min(m, n)). Each alignment is scanned once with a running streak, so the whole thing is O(m · n).

Spot it: A common subarray is a run of matches on one alignment (offset) of the two arrays. Sliding one array across the other and scanning each alignment for its longest run of equal elements is a window-style scan with O(1) memory.

Why not another pattern? The classic DP dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1 on matches is also O(m · n) but uses O(m · n) (or O(n)) memory. Binary search on the length with rolling hashes is O((m + n) log) but more complex.

Approach:

  1. For every offset (how far nums2 is shifted relative to nums1), walk the overlapping positions together.
  2. Keep run = length of the current streak of equal pairs; reset it on a mismatch.
  3. The best streak over all offsets is the answer.
class Solution:
    def findLength(self, nums1: List[int], nums2: List[int]) -> int:
        m = len(nums1)
        n = len(nums2)
        best = 0
        for offset in range(-(n - 1), m):  # nums2[j] lines up with nums1[j + offset]
            run = 0
            for j in range(n):
                i = j + offset
                if i < 0 or i >= m:
                    continue  # outside the overlap
                if nums1[i] == nums2[j]:
                    run = run + 1  # the matching streak continues
                    best = max(best, run)
                else:
                    run = 0  # a mismatch breaks the streak
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. offset covers every way of lining up the two arrays.
  2. For a fixed offset, a common subarray is a run of consecutive equal pairs.
  3. run counts the current streak; best keeps the longest streak seen on any alignment.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • No common elements → 0.
  • Identical arrays → their length.
  • The common part at the end of one array and the start of the other.

Complexity: O(m · n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 1343. Number of Sub-arrays of Size K and Average Greater than or Equal to Threshold Google Array

Problem: Count the subarrays of length k whose average is at least threshold.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: arr = [2,2,2,2,5,5,5,8], k = 3, threshold = 4
Output: 3
Explanation: Sub-arrays [2,5,5],[5,5,5] and [5,5,8] have averages 4, 5 and 6 respectively. All other sub-arrays of size 3 have averages less than 4 (the threshold).
Example 2
Input: arr = [11,13,17,23,29,31,7,5,2,3], k = 3, threshold = 5
Output: 6
Explanation: The first 6 sub-arrays of size 3 have averages greater than 5. Note that averages are not integers.

Constraints: 1 ≤ arr.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 10⁴ · 1 ≤ k ≤ arr.length · 0 ≤ threshold ≤ 10⁴

Hint 1

All windows have size k. How do you get the next window's sum from the previous one?

Hint 2

Compare the sum with k · threshold to avoid division.

From brute force to the pattern: Recomputing each window's sum is O(n · k). Updating it as the window slides is O(1) per step: O(n) total.

Spot it: Every window has the same size k: a fixed sliding window whose sum is updated in O(1) per step.

Why not another pattern? Summing each window from scratch is O(n · k). Prefix sums also give each window sum in O(1), at the cost of an extra array.

Approach:

  1. Compare sums instead of averages: average ≥ threshold ⇔ sum ≥ k · threshold (no division).
  2. Sum the first k elements.
  3. Slide: add the entering element, subtract the leaving one; count windows whose sum reaches the target.
class Solution:
    def numOfSubarrays(self, arr: List[int], k: int, threshold: int) -> int:
        target = k * threshold  # compare sums instead of averages
        window = sum(arr[:k])
        count = 1 if window >= target else 0
        for right in range(k, len(arr)):
            window = window + arr[right] - arr[right - k]  # slide by one
            if window >= target:
                count = count + 1
        return count

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. target = k * threshold: multiplying both sides by k avoids floating-point averages.
  2. window = sum(arr[:k]): the first window.
  3. Each slide adds arr[right] and removes arr[right - k], the element that just left.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k = n → one window.
  • threshold = 0 → every window counts.
  • k = 1 → count the elements ≥ threshold.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 1358. Number of Substrings Containing All Three Characters Google String

Problem: Count the substrings of s (made of a, b, c) that contain at least one of each letter.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "abcabc"
Output: 10
Explanation: The substrings containing at least one occurrence of the characters a, b and c are "abc", "abca", "abcab", "abcabc", "bca", "bcab", "bcabc", "cab", "cabc" and "abc" (again).
Example 2
Input: s = "aaacb"
Output: 3
Explanation: The substrings containing at least one occurrence of the characters a, b and c are "aaacb", "aacb" and "acb".

Constraints: 3 ≤ s.length ≤ 5 x 10⁴ · s only consists of 'a', 'b' or 'c' characters.

Hint 1

If s[i..j] contains all three letters, does s[i−1..j]?

Hint 2

For each right edge, shrink the window until it's no longer valid; the number of removed starts is the number of valid substrings.

From brute force to the pattern: Checking every substring for the three letters is O(n²). Validity is monotonic in the start position, so a window counts all valid starts for each end in amortised O(1).

Spot it: "At least one of each" is monotonic: once a window is valid, extending it stays valid. So for each right edge, find the largest left edge that still keeps it valid; every start at or before that edge works.

Why not another pattern? Checking every substring is O(n²). Tracking the last index of each letter is an even shorter equivalent (count += min(last) + 1).

Approach:

  1. Grow the window to the right, counting letters.
  2. While the window has all three letters, shrink from the left.
  3. After shrinking, left is the number of valid starts for this right edge (starts 0..left−1); add it.
class Solution:
    def numberOfSubstrings(self, s: str) -> int:
        count = {"a": 0, "b": 0, "c": 0}
        left = 0
        total = 0
        for right in range(len(s)):
            count[s[right]] = count[s[right]] + 1
            while count["a"] > 0 and count["b"] > 0 and count["c"] > 0:
                count[s[left]] = count[s[left]] - 1  # shrink while still containing all three
                left = left + 1
            total = total + left  # starts 0..left-1 all give a valid substring ending here
        return total

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. count holds the letters inside s[left..right].
  2. The while shrinks until the window is just missing one letter; at that point s[left − 1 .. right] was the shortest valid window.
  3. Any start from 0 to left − 1 gives a valid substring ending at right, so add left.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • A string missing a letter → 0.
  • "abc" → 1.
  • Long runs of one letter.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 1423. Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards Google Array

Problem: Take exactly k cards, each from the left or right end of the row. Maximise the total points.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: cardPoints = [1,2,3,4,5,6,1], k = 3
Output: 12
Explanation: After the first step, your score will always be 1. However, choosing the rightmost card first will maximize your total score. The optimal strategy is to take the three cards on the right, giving a final score of 1 + 6 + 5 = 12.
Example 2
Input: cardPoints = [2,2,2], k = 2
Output: 4
Explanation: Regardless of which two cards you take, your score will always be 4.

Constraints: 1 ≤ cardPoints.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ cardPoints[i] ≤ 10⁴ · 1 ≤ k ≤ cardPoints.length

Hint 1

After taking k cards from the ends, what shape do the remaining cards have?

Hint 2

They form a contiguous block of n − k. Find the block with the smallest sum.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying every sequence of left/right picks is 2ᵏ. Thinking about the leftover block turns it into a fixed sliding window: O(n).

Spot it: Whatever you take from the ends, the cards left over form one contiguous block of length n − k. Maximising what you take means minimising that block's sum: a fixed-size sliding window.

Why not another pattern? Trying every split (i from the left, k − i from the right) with prefix sums is also O(k) and equally good. Recursion over choices is exponential.

Approach:

  1. window = n − k. Sum the first window cards.
  2. Slide the window across, tracking the minimum window sum.
  3. Answer = total − minimum window sum.
class Solution:
    def maxScore(self, cardPoints: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        n = len(cardPoints)
        size = n - k  # the cards we leave behind form one block of this size
        total = sum(cardPoints)
        if size == 0:
            return total  # take everything
        window = sum(cardPoints[:size])
        smallest = window
        for right in range(size, n):
            window = window + cardPoints[right] - cardPoints[right - size]  # slide the block
            smallest = min(smallest, window)
        return total - smallest  # what's not left behind is what we took

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. size = n - k: the untouched middle block always has this length.
  2. if size == 0: taking all cards is the only option.
  3. The fixed window slides over all blocks of length size, tracking the smallest sum.
  4. total - smallest: the best score.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k = n → the total.
  • k = 1 → the larger end card.
  • All cards equal.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 1461. Check If a String Contains All Binary Codes of Size K Google StringHash Set

Problem: Return True if every binary string of length k appears as a substring of s.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "00110110", k = 2
Output: true
Explanation: The binary codes of length 2 are "00", "01", "10" and "11". They can be all found as substrings at indices 0, 1, 3 and 2 respectively.
Example 2
Input: s = "0110", k = 1
Output: true
Explanation: The binary codes of length 1 are "0" and "1", it is clear that both exist as a substring.

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 5 * 10⁵ · s[i] is either '0' or '1'. · 1 ≤ k ≤ 20

Hint 1

Every length-k substring is a window. How many distinct codes are needed?

Hint 2

Encode each window as an integer that you update in O(1) as the window slides.

From brute force to the pattern: Slicing every window costs O(k) each; a rolling integer makes each step O(1), so the scan is O(n).

Spot it: All substrings of length k are the windows of a fixed size. A rolling bit value (shift left, add the new bit, mask to k bits) gives each window's code in O(1); collect them in a set and check whether there are 2ᵏ of them.

Why not another pattern? Slicing each window as a string is O(k) per window. Generating all 2ᵏ codes and searching for each is O(2ᵏ · n).

Approach:

  1. If there are fewer than 2ᵏ windows, return False early.
  2. Keep value = the last k bits as an integer: value = ((value << 1) & mask) | bit.
  3. Once at least k bits have been read, add value to a set.
  4. Return whether the set has 2ᵏ codes.
class Solution:
    def hasAllCodes(self, s: str, k: int) -> bool:
        need = 1 << k  # 2^k different codes
        if len(s) - k + 1 < need:
            return False  # not enough windows to contain every code
        mask = need - 1  # keeps only the last k bits
        seen = set()
        value = 0
        for i in range(len(s)):
            value = ((value << 1) & mask) | (s[i] == "1")  # slide the k-bit window
            if i >= k - 1:
                seen.add(value)  # the window s[i-k+1 .. i]
        return len(seen) == need

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. 1 << k is 2ᵏ; with fewer windows than that, some code must be missing.
  2. (value << 1) & mask: shift in a new bit and drop the oldest one; | (s[i] == "1") adds the new bit (True counts as 1).
  3. From index k − 1 on, value encodes a full window.
  4. Distinct window codes are collected in seen.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k larger than len(s) → False.
  • k = 1: both 0 and 1 must appear.
  • Many repeated windows.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(2ᵏ) space.

Medium 1695. Maximum Erasure Value Google ArrayHash Set

Problem: Erase one subarray with all unique elements; its score is the sum of its elements. Return the maximum score.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [4,2,4,5,6]
Output: 17
Explanation: The optimal subarray here is [2,4,5,6].
Example 2
Input: nums = [5,2,1,2,5,2,1,2,5]
Output: 8
Explanation: The optimal subarray here is [5,2,1] or [1,2,5].

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴

Hint 1

This is "longest substring without repeating characters" with sums.

Hint 2

Keep a set of values in the window and a running sum; shrink from the left when a duplicate arrives.

From brute force to the pattern: Summing every unique subarray is O(n²). A window that only moves forward handles each element twice: O(n).

Spot it: "Contiguous + all unique" is the Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters window, keeping a running sum instead of a length.

Why not another pattern? Checking every subarray is O(n²). Prefix sums alone can't enforce uniqueness. The window works because all values are positive: extending a valid window can only increase its sum, so the best window ending at each position is the longest unique one.

Approach:

  1. Grow the window to the right, adding to window_sum.
  2. If the new value is already in the window, remove from the left until it isn't.
  3. Track the best window_sum.
class Solution:
    def maximumUniqueSubarray(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        inside = set()  # values currently in the window
        left = 0
        window_sum = 0
        best = 0
        for x in nums:
            while x in inside:
                inside.remove(nums[left])  # drop from the left until x is unique
                window_sum = window_sum - nums[left]
                left = left + 1
            inside.add(x)
            window_sum = window_sum + x
            best = max(best, window_sum)
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. inside is the set of values in the window, so the uniqueness check is O(1).
  2. The while removes elements from the left until the old copy of x is gone.
  3. Add x and update the running sum and the best score.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • All values distinct → the whole sum.
  • All values equal → that value.
  • A duplicate far back in the window.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 1838. Frequency of the Most Frequent Element Google Array

Problem: In one operation you can increment any element by 1. With at most k operations, maximise the frequency of some element.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,4], k = 5
Output: 3
Explanation: Increment the first element three times and the second element two times to make nums = [4,4,4]. 4 has a frequency of 3.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,4,8,13], k = 5
Output: 2
Explanation: There are multiple optimal solutions: - Increment the first element three times to make nums = [4,4,8,13]. 4 has a frequency of 2. - Increment the second element four times to make nums = [1,8,8,13]. 8 has a frequency of 2. - Increment the third element five times to make nums = [1,4,13,13]. 13 has a frequency of 2.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ k ≤ 10⁵

Hint 1

Which elements would you raise to match a chosen value? Think about the sorted order.

Hint 2

Use a window over the sorted array whose cost is nums[right] × size − sum.

From brute force to the pattern: For every target value, raising the closest smaller values greedily is O(n²). Sorting makes the cost of a window easy to compute, and the window only moves forward: O(n log n) total.

Spot it: After sorting, it's best to raise a contiguous block of values up to its largest element. The cost of a window [left, right] is nums[right] × size − window_sum, which only grows when the window grows: a variable sliding window.

Why not another pattern? For each target value, binary-searching the farthest start with prefix sums is O(n log n) after sorting; the window is O(n) after sorting.

Approach:

  1. Sort nums.
  2. Extend right, adding to window_sum.
  3. While raising everything in the window to nums[right] costs more than k, remove nums[left].
  4. Track the longest window.
class Solution:
    def maxFrequency(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        nums = sorted(nums)
        left = 0
        window_sum = 0
        best = 0
        for right in range(len(nums)):
            window_sum = window_sum + nums[right]
            # cost to raise every element of the window up to nums[right]
            while nums[right] * (right - left + 1) - window_sum > k:
                window_sum = window_sum - nums[left]  # too expensive: drop the smallest
                left = left + 1
            best = max(best, right - left + 1)
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Sorting puts the cheapest values to raise right next to the target.
  2. nums[right] * size - window_sum is exactly how many increments the window needs.
  3. If that exceeds k, drop the leftmost (smallest) element, which is the most expensive to raise.

Edge cases to test:

  • k = 0 → the highest existing frequency.
  • All equal values → n.
  • Large k that can raise everything → n.

Complexity: O(n log n) time for the sort, O(n) for the window.

Medium 1888. Minimum Number of Flips to Make the Binary String Alternating Google String

Problem: You may rotate s (move the first character to the end) any number of times, then flip characters. Return the minimum number of flips to make s alternating.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "111000"
Output: 2
Explanation: Use the first operation two times to make s = "100011". Then, use the second operation on the third and sixth elements to make s = "101010".
Example 2
Input: s = "010"
Output: 0
Explanation: The string is already alternating.

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁵ · s[i] is either '0' or '1'.

Hint 1

What do all rotations of s have in common with s + s?

Hint 2

Slide a window of length n over s + s, counting mismatches against both alternating patterns.

From brute force to the pattern: For each of the n rotations, counting mismatches is O(n): O(n²). In s + s consecutive rotations differ by one character in and one out, so the counts update in O(1).

Spot it: Every rotation of s is a window of length n in s + s. Compare each window with the two alternating patterns: the number of mismatches changes by at most one character in and one out as the window slides.

Why not another pattern? Rebuilding each rotation and counting mismatches is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. Let t = s + s; every rotation of s is one window of length n in t.
  2. Slide a window of length n over t, keeping mismatch counts against both patterns 0101… and 1010….
  3. Each full window gives a candidate: the smaller of the two counts.
class Solution:
    def minFlips(self, s: str) -> int:
        n = len(s)
        t = s + s  # every rotation is a window of length n
        diff_a = 0  # mismatches against "0101..."
        diff_b = 0  # mismatches against "1010..."
        best = n
        for i in range(len(t)):
            expect_a = "0" if i % 2 == 0 else "1"
            if t[i] != expect_a:
                diff_a = diff_a + 1
            else:
                diff_b = diff_b + 1  # matching "0101..." means mismatching "1010..."
            if i >= n:  # the character at i - n leaves the window
                old = t[i - n]
                old_expect_a = "0" if (i - n) % 2 == 0 else "1"
                if old != old_expect_a:
                    diff_a = diff_a - 1
                else:
                    diff_b = diff_b - 1
            if i >= n - 1:
                best = min(best, diff_a, diff_b)  # a full rotation is in the window
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. t = s + s: rotating by r gives t[r : r + n].
  2. The patterns are fixed to positions in t; a window starting at an odd index simply uses them shifted, which is why both patterns are tracked.
  3. Each character either matches pattern A or pattern B, so exactly one of the two counters goes up.
  4. When the window is longer than n, the character leaving it is removed from whichever counter it was in.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Already alternating → 0.
  • Odd length (rotation actually helps), e.g. "111000" → 2.
  • A single character → 0.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for s + s.

Medium 2461. Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K Google ArrayHash Map

Problem: Among subarrays of length k whose elements are all distinct, return the maximum sum (0 if none).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,5,4,2,9,9,9], k = 3
Output: 15
Explanation: The subarrays of nums with length 3 are: - [1,5,4] which meets the requirements and has a sum of 10. - [5,4,2] which meets the requirements and has a sum of 11. - [4,2,9] which meets the requirements and has a sum of 15. - [2,9,9] which does not meet the requirements because the element 9 is repeated. - [9,9,9] which does not meet the requirements because the element 9 is repeated. We return 15 because it is the maximum subarray sum of all the subarrays that meet the conditions
Example 2
Input: nums = [4,4,4], k = 3
Output: 0
Explanation: The subarrays of nums with length 3 are: - [4,4,4] which does not meet the requirements because the element 4 is repeated. We return 0 because no subarrays meet the conditions.

Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁵

Hint 1

All windows have length k. How can you tell if a window has no duplicates?

Hint 2

Keep a count map of the window; it has no duplicates exactly when it has k keys.

From brute force to the pattern: Checking each window with a fresh set is O(n · k). A count map updated as the window slides is O(1) per step.

Spot it: Fixed-length windows (k) with a property of their contents (all distinct): slide the window and keep counts of the values inside.

Why not another pattern? Rebuilding a set for every window is O(n · k). A count map updated by one add and one remove per slide is O(1) per step.

Approach:

  1. Slide a window of size k, keeping count of each value and the window sum.
  2. When a value's count drops to 0, delete it, so len(count) is the number of distinct values.
  3. If len(count) == k, the window is valid: update the best sum.
class Solution:
    def maximumSubarraySum(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        count = {}  # value -> occurrences inside the window
        window_sum = 0
        best = 0
        for right in range(len(nums)):
            x = nums[right]
            count[x] = count.get(x, 0) + 1
            window_sum = window_sum + x
            if right >= k:
                old = nums[right - k]  # the element leaving the window
                count[old] = count[old] - 1
                if count[old] == 0:
                    del count[old]
                window_sum = window_sum - old
            if right >= k - 1 and len(count) == k:
                best = max(best, window_sum)  # all k values are distinct
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Add the entering element to count and to the sum.
  2. Once the window is longer than k, remove nums[right - k]; deleting zero counts keeps len(count) equal to the number of distinct values.
  3. A full window with k distinct keys has no duplicates.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • No valid window → 0.
  • k = 1 → the maximum element.
  • A duplicate that enters and leaves the window.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(k) space.

Medium 2958. Length of Longest Subarray With at Most K Frequency Google ArrayHash Map

Problem: Return the length of the longest subarray in which every value occurs at most k times.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,3,1,2,3,1,2], k = 2
Output: 6
Explanation: The longest possible good subarray is [1,2,3,1,2,3] since the values 1, 2, and 3 occur at most twice in this subarray. Note that the subarrays [2,3,1,2,3,1] and [3,1,2,3,1,2] are also good. It can be shown that there are no good subarrays with length more than 6.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,2,1,2,1,2,1,2], k = 1
Output: 2
Explanation: The longest possible good subarray is [1,2] since the values 1 and 2 occur at most once in this subarray. Note that the subarray [2,1] is also good. It can be shown that there are no good subarrays with length more than 2.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹ · 1 ≤ k ≤ nums.length

Hint 1

When you add a new element to a valid window, which value could break the rule?

Hint 2

Shrink from the left until that value's count is at most k.

From brute force to the pattern: Counting frequencies for every subarray is O(n²). The window keeps counts incrementally and each index moves at most twice: O(n).

Spot it: Longest contiguous window satisfying a frequency limit: a variable sliding window. The only value that can exceed k after adding nums[right] is nums[right] itself, so shrink until its count is back to k.

Why not another pattern? Checking every subarray is O(n²). Binary search on the length with a check per length is O(n log n); the window is linear.

Approach:

  1. Add nums[right] to the counts.
  2. While its count exceeds k, remove nums[left] and move left right.
  3. Track the longest window.
class Solution:
    def maxSubarrayLength(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        count = {}
        left = 0
        best = 0
        for right in range(len(nums)):
            x = nums[right]
            count[x] = count.get(x, 0) + 1
            while count[x] > k:
                count[nums[left]] = count[nums[left]] - 1  # shrink until x is allowed again
                left = left + 1
            best = max(best, right - left + 1)
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. count tracks frequencies inside the window.
  2. Only x can have just gone over the limit, so the loop shrinks until count[x] ≤ k.
  3. right - left + 1 is the current valid window length.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k ≥ n → the whole array.
  • All elements equal → k.
  • k = 1 → the longest subarray of distinct values.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 3356. Zero Array Transformation II Google Array

Problem: Query [l, r, val] lets you decrement each element in l..r by up to val. Return the smallest k such that the first k queries can turn nums into all zeros, or −1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [2,0,2], queries = [[0,2,1],[0,2,1],[1,1,3]]
Output: 2
Explanation: For i = 0 (l = 0, r = 2, val = 1): Decrement values at indices [0, 1, 2] by [1, 0, 1] respectively. The array will become [1, 0, 1]. For i = 1 (l = 0, r = 2, val = 1): Decrement values at indices [0, 1, 2] by [1, 0, 1] respectively. The array will become [0, 0, 0], which is a Zero Array. Therefore, the minimum value of k is 2.
Example 2
Input: nums = [4,3,2,1], queries = [[1,3,2],[0,2,1]]
Output: -1
Explanation: For i = 0 (l = 1, r = 3, val = 2): Decrement values at indices [1, 2, 3] by [2, 2, 1] respectively. The array will become [4, 1, 0, 0]. For i = 1 (l = 0, r = 2, val = 1): Decrement values at indices [0, 1, 2] by [1, 1, 0] respectively. The array will become [3, 0, 0, 0], which is not a Zero Array.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 5 * 10⁵ · 1 ≤ queries.length ≤ 10⁵ · queries[i].length == 3 · 0 ≤ li ≤ ri < nums.length · 1 ≤ vali ≤ 5

Hint 1

Process the array from left to right. When do you need another query?

Hint 2

Keep the available decrement at index i with a difference array, and add queries one by one until it reaches nums[i].

From brute force to the pattern: Trying each k and simulating all k queries is O(q · (n + q)). Because the first k queries are always used in order, one left-to-right sweep that pulls queries only when needed finds the minimum k in O(n + q).

Spot it: Walk the array left to right keeping how much decrement is available at the current index. Whenever it's not enough, pull in the next query; queries only ever move forward, so this is a two-pointer sweep with a difference array for the ranges.

Why not another pattern? Binary search on k with a difference-array check per guess is O((n + q) log q) and also fine; the sweep avoids the log factor.

Approach:

  1. diff records where each applied query's decrement starts and stops; power is the running sum at index i.
  2. At index i, add diff[i] to power.
  3. While power < nums[i]: apply query k. If it covers i, it contributes now (power += val) and stops after r; if it starts later, record it in diff. If no queries are left, return −1.
  4. After the sweep, k is the answer.
class Solution:
    def minZeroArray(self, nums: List[int], queries: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(nums)
        diff = [0] * (n + 1)  # decrement starting/stopping at each index
        power = 0  # total decrement available at the current index
        k = 0  # number of queries used so far
        for i in range(n):
            power = power + diff[i]
            while power < nums[i]:
                if k == len(queries):
                    return -1  # every query used and nums[i] still can't reach 0
                l, r, val = queries[k]
                k = k + 1
                if r < i:
                    continue  # this query only covers indices we've already handled
                start = max(l, i)
                if start == i:
                    power = power + val  # covers i right now
                else:
                    diff[start] = diff[start] + val  # starts later
                diff[r + 1] = diff[r + 1] - val  # stops after r
        return k

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. power is the sum of val over the applied queries that cover index i (a running prefix sum of diff).
  2. The while pulls in queries in order only when needed, so k ends as small as possible.
  3. A query that ends before i is still "processed" (it counts toward k) but can't help anymore.
  4. Queries starting at or before i add to power immediately; later ones are scheduled in diff. All of them stop at r + 1.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Already all zeros → 0.
  • Not enough total decrement → −1.
  • A query that ends before the index that needs it (it still counts toward k).

Complexity: O(n + q) time, O(n) space.
